description: We’re Dorment Crew, six teammates from the NASA Space Apps event in Virudhunagar, India. We brought our skills in research, storytelling, and coding together to build ECHOES. Our idea began with a question: what can a rover teach us after its last signal? In our game, young explorers follow clues across the Moon and Mars, using real NASA photos to discover the stories behind the machines left there.
summary: Dorment Crew built ECHOES – The Last Transmission, a cinematic browser game about the spacecraft and scientific instruments left behind after their missions. In a fictional 2026 expedition, players explore the Moon as astronaut Yuva and Mars through the camera of E.D.I.T.H., a robotic explorer. At each waypoint, they inspect real NASA photographs and mission records to learn what the equipment discovered and why its signals stopped. The story follows Surveyor 3 and Opportunity, then brings the crew back to Earth for an interview where players test what they learned. ECHOES gives old hardware a new role as evidence players can investigate, showing how those missions still help us understand the Moon and Mars.
details:
ECHOES – The Last Transmission is an interactive story about the machines humans have left on the Moon and Mars. We built it around a simple question: What can we learn from a machine after it stops sending signals? The game uses real NASA photographs and mission records to help players discover what these machines did and how they shaped space exploration.

The story. In our fictional mission set in 2026, astronaut Yuva and an AI robot named E.D.I.T.H. train together before launching on the same rocket. Their vehicles separate in space. Yuva heads to the Moon to investigate Surveyor 3, a robotic lander that helped scientists learn about the lunar surface before astronauts landed there. E.D.I.T.H. heads to Mars to investigate Opportunity, a rover that sent back evidence that water once played a role in shaping the planet. The story follows both characters as they uncover what happened to the equipment and complete their mission.

What players do. The experience begins with voiced cutscenes. When Yuva lands, players take control of her and follow markers across the Moon. At each stop, they can open an inspection panel with a real NASA photograph and a short explanation of the equipment. The story then shifts to Mars, where players explore through E.D.I.T.H.’s camera. Players can move using the keyboard or on-screen buttons, and a guided navigation option helps them find the next stop.

How the story ends. On the return journey, Yuva and E.D.I.T.H. hear a news report about Voyager. The film shows how Yuva imagines the probes traveling through deep space. Back on Earth, she gives a televised interview. Players answer six short questions during the interview to see what they remember from the mission.

Why we built it this way. Space mission records can be hard to follow if you’re new to the topic. We wanted someone with no background in space science to walk up to a piece of equipment, see what it looked like, and understand why it mattered. The fictional journey gives players a reason to explore, while the inspection panels explain the real history. Switching between Yuva and E.D.I.T.H. also gives players two ways to experience the mission: walking on the Moon as an astronaut and seeing Mars through a robot’s camera.

What we used. We built the website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and used Three.js to create the 3D environments players explore. We used FFmpeg to prepare the cutscene videos and Kokoro to generate the narration. NASA and JPL resources informed the equipment histories. We hosted the finished game on Vercel so it can be played in a browser. Captions, touch controls, guided navigation, and saved checkpoints help players follow the story and return to where they left off.
